title: Problem 1
statement_text: What is the minimum number of transpositions needed in a $t$-reachable network? What if all transpositions are of the form $(1,\cdot)$?
context_text: A sequence of transpositions $T_1,\dots,T_\ell$ of $[n]$, $T_i=(a_i,b_i)$, is a $t$-reachability network ($t$-reachable network) if for every choice of $t$ distinct ordered points $x_1,\dots,x_t\in[n]$ some subsequence $T_{i_1},\dots,T_{i_{\ell'}}$ has composition $(a_{i_1},b_{i_1})\cdots(a_{i_{\ell'}},b_{i_{\ell'}})$ mapping $j\mapsto x_j$ for $1\le j\le t$; informally, $t$ counters starting at positions $1,\dots,t$ can be moved to any prescribed positions by performing or skipping each transposition in turn. An $n$-reachability network is a permutation network, which needs $\Theta(n\log n)$ transpositions (Waksman). Star transpositions are those of the form $(1,\cdot)$. For $t=1$, exactly $n-1$ transpositions are needed. The authors prove that the shortest $2$-reachability network has exactly $\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$ transpositions, and $\lceil3(n-1)/2\rceil$ when only star transpositions are allowed ($n\ge3$); for every $t\ge3$, a randomised construction gives $t$-reachability networks of length $(2+o_t(1))n$, with leading coefficient independent of $t$ (using star transpositions apart from a final network on the first $t$ positions). For star transpositions they prove a lower bound $(2-1/t)n-C_t$, tight up to additive constants for $t=2,3$. Even the asymptotics of the minimum length for large $t$ remain open, and there is still a gap between upper and lower bounds in the star case.

title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: For $n\geq 2$, the minimum number of lazy transpositions in a 2-uniformity network is $2n-3$.
context_text: A sequence of transpositions $T_1,\dots,T_\ell$ of $[n]$, $T_i=(a_i,b_i)$, is a $t$-reachability network ($t$-reachable network) if for every choice of $t$ distinct ordered points $x_1,\dots,x_t\in[n]$ some subsequence $T_{i_1},\dots,T_{i_{\ell'}}$ has composition $(a_{i_1},b_{i_1})\cdots(a_{i_{\ell'}},b_{i_{\ell'}})$ mapping $j\mapsto x_j$ for $1\le j\le t$; informally, $t$ counters starting at positions $1,\dots,t$ can be moved to any prescribed positions by performing or skipping each transposition in turn. An $n$-reachability network is a permutation network, which needs $\Theta(n\log n)$ transpositions (Waksman). Star transpositions are those of the form $(1,\cdot)$. A lazy transposition $(a,b,p)$ is the random permutation equal to $(a,b)$ with probability $p$ and to the identity otherwise. A sequence of independent lazy transpositions $T_1,\dots,T_\ell$ is a $t$-uniformity network if the probability that $T_1\cdots T_\ell$ maps $(1,\dots,t)$ to $(x_1,\dots,x_t)$ is the same for every tuple of $t$ distinct elements of $[n]$; every $t$-uniformity network yields a $t$-reachability network, and the shortest $2$-reachability network has $\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$ transpositions. The authors construct a $2$-uniformity network of length $2n-3$: $(1,2,\frac12),(1,3,\frac2n),(1,2,\frac12),(1,4,\frac2{n-1}),\dots,(1,2,\frac12),(1,n,\frac23),(1,2,\frac12)$, prove that $2$-uniformity networks using only star transpositions need at least $1.6n-C$ of them, and conjecture that $2n-3$ is optimal (it would match nicely with selection networks). A footnote in the final version states that, after a preliminary version was put on arXiv, this conjecture was proven by Janzer, Johnson and Leader ('Partial shuffles by lazy swaps'), which also separates $2$-reachability from $2$-uniformity without the star restriction.
notes: The paper states that after a preliminary version was posted on arXiv, Conjecture 1 was proven (by unspecified authors in the truncated text); it may no longer be open.
